segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Social Dialogue

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Hello, is this the temporary library help point?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It is. I'm Owen, one of the library assistants. How can I help?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm Priya. I'm a second-year student in the biology department. I've just moved into the halls of residence, and I'm completely lost.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Don't worry, you're not the first. The Hartley Building is closed, so everything has been moved to the old sports hall.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Right. So where exactly is that?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It's on the north edge of the campus, next to the boathouse. If you come out of the main teaching building, turn left at the fountain, and follow the path past the car park. It takes about twelve minutes on foot.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Twelve minutes. That's not too bad. And can I still borrow books?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, you can. But most of the collection is in storage, so you request items online and collect them here the next working day. The request service is free.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Good. What about the opening hours?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: We open at eight in the morning on weekdays and close at eleven at night. At weekends we open at nine and close at eight.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's later than I expected.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, the college extended the hours because of the complaints. There's also a minibus after nine in the evening, every half hour, back to the halls.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Perfect. Is there anywhere quiet to study?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: There's a silent zone at the eastern end of the hall, and a separate quiet reading room with forty seats. But the silent zone fills up quickly, so come before ten if you want a place.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Understood. Is there a café?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: There is, run by the students' union. It's small, and it closes at six. There's also a vending machine near the entrance.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: One more thing. I have a presentation next week, and I need a quiet room to rehearse. Can I book one?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Not in the temporary building, I'm afraid. The group study rooms are all in the Hartley Building, and they won't reopen until August. But you can book a small seminar room in the teaching building through the student portal.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'll do that. Thanks, Owen.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You're welcome. And good luck with the presentation.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Social Monologue

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. This is a recorded message from the Northgate College volunteering office about the autumn bird survey. The survey is part of a national citizen science project, and we need volunteers from across the college.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The survey runs for three weekends, starting on Saturday the fourth of October and finishing on Sunday the nineteenth. Volunteers are asked to choose a short route of about one kilometre, either on campus or in the streets near their accommodation, and to walk it slowly once a week, early in the morning, starting at seven o'clock. Each walk takes about ten minutes, but please allow half an hour in total for recording your results.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You do not need to be an expert. We will provide a simple identification guide and a free one-hour training session, which will be held in the teaching building on the evening of Wednesday the first of October, from six until seven. Please bring a phone if you have one, because the records are submitted through a mobile application. If you do not have a smartphone, paper forms are available at the help point.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There is one important rule. Please record only the species you are confident about. If you are unsure, mark the sighting as uncertain, and an expert will check it later. This may feel like you are providing less information, but it makes the data much more reliable.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: At the end of the survey, all volunteers will receive a summary map showing the birds recorded in their area, and the three volunteers who record the most species will receive a small book about urban wildlife. To join, sign up at the volunteering office by Friday the twenty-sixth of September, or send an email to the address on the college website. Thank you, and we hope to see you at the training session.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Academic Discussion

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Come in, both of you. Sit down. So, this is your mid-project review. Daniel, let's start with you. Remind me what you're working on.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: I'm looking at how students prepare for oral presentations, and whether rehearsal actually improves their performance.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Right. And Mei, your project?

segments.speaker: Mei
segments.text: Mine is about the bird survey. I'm investigating whether volunteers record more species as they become more experienced.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Those are quite different, but both involve observation. Daniel, what have you found so far?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: I've interviewed four tutors, and I've recorded three student presentations. The tutors all said that delivery matters more than accent, which surprised me.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's consistent with what I've read. But four tutors is a small sample. You should be careful about generalising.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Yes, I know. I'm hoping to interview two more before the end of the month.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. And Mei, how is the data collection going?

segments.speaker: Mei
segments.text: It's going well, but I've hit a problem. Some volunteers are much more skilled than others, so the number of birds they record goes up over time. I'm not sure whether that's a real change in the birds or just a change in the observers.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's a well-known issue. It's usually called observer effort. Have you thought about how to deal with it?

segments.speaker: Mei
segments.text: I was thinking of comparing each volunteer's first walk with their last walk, rather than comparing volunteers with each other.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's a sensible approach. It controls for differences between people. Daniel, does your project have a similar problem?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: A bit. The students who volunteered to be recorded might be more confident than the ones who didn't.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Exactly. That's a self-selection problem. You should mention it in your limitations section. Now, let's talk about the write-up. The draft is due on the fourteenth of November, and the final version on the twelfth of December. Mei, have you started writing?

segments.speaker: Mei
segments.text: I've written the methods section, but not the discussion.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Start with the limitations, then. It's often easier to write when you know what you can't claim. And Daniel, don't leave the conclusion until the last minute. One more thing: both of you need to submit an ethics form before you do any more interviews or observations. The deadline for that is the thirtieth of September.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: We've already submitted ours.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Then I'll see you both in two weeks.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: Academic Lecture

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to explain how a peer-review workshop is organised in our department, and why we run it the way we do. This is a practical lecture, so I'll describe the stages in order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, a word about purpose. A peer-review workshop is a meeting in which students read and comment on each other's drafts before those drafts are submitted for assessment. It is not a marking session, and students are not asked to give grades. The aim is to help the writer see what a reader actually understands, which is often different from what the writer intended.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Second, the preparation stage. About ten days before the workshop, each student uploads a draft of no more than two thousand words to the shared folder. Everyone is then assigned two drafts to read, and these assignments are made by the tutor, not chosen by the students, so that friends do not automatically review each other. Readers are given a short form with three questions: what is the main argument, which section is least clear, and what evidence is missing. The form is deliberately simple, because open-ended comments tend to be vague.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Third, the workshop itself. We meet for ninety minutes. In the first twenty minutes, each writer describes their draft in two minutes and then listens without speaking while the two readers give their comments. The writer may take notes but may not argue. This rule, which some students find frustrating at first, is designed to make the writer listen rather than defend. In the remaining time, the group discusses two or three common problems that appeared in several drafts.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Fourth, the follow-up. Within three days of the workshop, each writer produces a short revision plan of about two hundred words, listing the changes they intend to make and the reasons for them. The plan is submitted to the tutor, who comments on it briefly. The revised draft is then submitted for assessment two weeks later. Students are not required to accept the readers' suggestions, but they are required to explain why they accepted or rejected them.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Why do we insist on this process? There are three reasons. Firstly, readers notice problems that writers cannot see in their own work, particularly problems of structure. Secondly, the discipline of commenting on someone else's writing improves the commenter's own writing, because it makes them more aware of how texts are organised. Thirdly, the revision plan creates a record of thinking, which is useful when a student later asks for feedback or appeals a mark.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There are, of course, limitations. Students sometimes give comments that are too general, such as 'it's good' or 'it needs more detail'. We try to reduce this by giving examples of useful comments in the first session. Some students also feel that the process takes too much time, and it is true that it adds about four hours of work per draft. However, the department's own review of results found that students who attended at least two workshops in a term improved their marks by an average of six per cent, compared with those who attended none. That figure should be treated with caution, because attendance is voluntary and motivated students may simply work harder anyway.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: In conclusion, the workshop is designed to make writing visible: it turns a private activity into a structured conversation. Next week, we will look at how to write the revision plan itself, and I will show you two examples, one strong and one weak. Please bring your drafts to that session.
